chapter_theme: The hero goes on winning wives by his mantra-rite (Menaki of Ujjayini, Srimati of Madurai, Madanamanjari, Ilakkanai), kills the Vidyadhara Vayuvegan who killed the Prithivitilaka king and seized his five hundred daughters, and at the end meets a sage and asks him the cause of his fortune.

cast.role: the hero, who wins brides by the mantra-rite
the hero's brother or companion of Pataliputra, who tells him of Menaki
daughter of King Jayasena of Ujjayini
the merchant who tells of Bhutilaka
the leader of the five hundred singing Vidyadhara women
the Vidyadhara who kills the women's father and seizes the kingdom
the five hundred brothers of the women, who become the hero's servants
the ancient sages who come to the grove
the Charana sage who teaches the hero dharma

124.reading: A verse whose first half is too corrupt to follow says that someone, after seeing a flaw, came and, failing to get the women he asked for, killed the king of the city of the white banner.
124.nuance: The first two lines are unclear (மேகவா கனன்றுரந்திட, கள்ளவிழ் மாசுகண்டனவன்) and the subject of the killing is not named; whether it is a foe of the hero, an earlier episode retold, or the hero himself cannot be fixed here.
124.event: An unnamed figure kills the king of the white-bannered city after failing to obtain the women he asked for.

125.reading: The king's younger brother, wanting the hero, sends a letter; once the hero has understood what the letter says, he turns the peacock-feathered arrow and kills the man who came.
125.nuance: The line breaks and the word நாந்தக (a sword name elsewhere) make the sense of lines 2 to 3 uncertain; who sent the letter and who is killed is read from the sentence order only.
125.event: The hero reads the letter brought to him, reworks an arrow and kills the man who had come with it.

126.reading: Going secretly to Abhichandra's city on an auspicious day, the hero marries the daughters of Subhachandra and Abhichandra's own daughter Sukanda by means of a mantra-rite, and is glad.
126.nuance: வேள்வி here is a rite performed with mantras (செபமந்திர வேள்வி) to win the women, not a Vedic sacrifice; the poem uses it again at 131, 139, 141 and 143 as the hero's way of taking brides.
126.event: The hero goes to Abhichandra's city and marries Subhachandra's daughters and Abhichandra's daughter by a mantra-rite.

127.reading: With the women as his companions the hero, joyful, takes his pleasure and plays on the pleasure-hill outside the swelling city.
127.event: The hero enjoys himself with his wives at a pleasure-hill outside the city.

128.reading: The text introduces Ujjayini in the land of Avanti, its king Jayasena, his wife Jayasri and their golden-hued daughter Menaki.
128.nuance: The last line names the daughter without a verb: the sentence is left open and finished in 129 to 131.

129.reading: Mavyalan of Pataliputra has come to Ujjayini; a Vidyadhara woman (சேடி) comes to tell Menaki of him, and she sees him and goes to the garden-wall of the treasure-city.
129.nuance: Who goes to the wall (நன்னிதிப் புரிசை) and why is not clear from the Tamil: நன்னிதி may be a name or an epithet, and the second half may refer to Menaki or to a different woman.
129.event: Mavyalan arrives in Ujjayini, and Menaki, told of him by a Vidyadhara woman, goes to him.

130.reading: Mavyalan leaves that city, goes to his elder brother and bows at his feet, and when the younger brother is asked where the hero is, he answers.
130.nuance: Line 3 to 4 make the pairing of 'elder brother' and 'hero' unclear: the Tamil can be read as the hero himself being the elder brother, and the questioner is not named.
130.event: Mavyalan leaves Ujjayini, bows to his elder brother and is asked about Nagakumara.

131.reading: Mavyalan tells of Menaki, slender-waisted and like the love-god's own beauty, and the hero goes to that city and weds her by the mantra-rite.
131.nuance: Mavyalan's words are the report of Menaki's beauty in lines 1 to 2; the marriage in lines 3 to 4 is the narrator's.
131.event: The hero hears from Mavyalan of Menaki, goes to Ujjayini and marries her by a mantra-rite.

132.reading: Another tale is told of Madurai, where the dancer Srimati, skilled in the drama and its victorious drums, has declared that whoever overcomes her will be her husband.
132.nuance: The speaker of line 1 (மற்றுமொன்று உரைத்தனன்) is not named; he is taken to be Mavyalan from 131. The last line is the sense of a challenge (பதியாம் பார்மிசை) and rests on a damaged word division.
132.event: A tale is told of the Madurai dancer Srimati, who will take as husband the man who defeats her.

133.reading: The hero goes there, beats her and takes her, lives with the women, then asks a merchant come by ship to tell him where a wonder is to be found.
133.nuance: The hero's question is in lines 3 and 4 (எங்குள அதிசயம் இயம்புக நீ).
133.event: The hero defeats Srimati and takes her, then asks an arriving merchant about marvels.

134.reading: The merchant answers that on the sea stands Bhutilaka, a city whose temple of the Lord has five hundred women singing daily as instructed, and he does not know why.
134.nuance: புங்கவன் (the Lord) is the Jina by the poem's frame (the temple is called அருகனாலயம் in 136), but the verse does not say so.
134.event: The merchant tells of a sea-island city where five hundred women sing daily at a temple.

135.reading: Remembering his own vidya, the hero goes with his chosen friends to the island, sees and circles the golden temple, and bows before the Jina.
135.nuance: வள்ளல் is the hero; the vidya he calls to mind (வித்தை) is the learned flying power by which he crosses the sea, though the verse does not say what it does.
135.event: The hero, with companions, flies to the island, circles the golden temple and worships.

136.reading: The hero, hearing the women sing in a line, calls them over and asks who they are to cry out before the Arhat temple, and Dharanisundari answers.
136.nuance: தரணிசுந் தரி is split across words by the edition; the speaker form in line 4 is as written.
136.event: The hero summons the singing women and asks who they are; Dharanisundari begins to answer.

137.reading: Dharanisundari says they are from the Vidyadhara city Prithivitilaka on the great silver mountain, where Vayuvegan asked their father to give them to his nephew.
137.nuance: மருகன் (nephew or son-in-law) leaves open whether the women were to marry Vayuvegan's nephew; the sentence at line 3 is loosely joined.
137.event: Dharanisundari tells where she and the others come from and that Vayuvegan demanded them for his nephew.

138.reading: Because their father refused, she says, Vayuvegan raged like fire, killed him, seized their kingdom and settled in the forest, and on hearing this the hero kills Vayuvegan.
138.nuance: The verse treats the hero's killing as the answer to Vayuvegan's, without remark; the poem does not ask whether the Jain rule against killing bears on it.
138.event: Vayuvegan, refused, kills the women's father and seizes the kingdom; the hero then kills Vayuvegan.

139.reading: The hero wins the five hundred women by the mantra-rite and enjoys them with love, and their five hundred brothers come as his servants and, worshipping him as refuge, live content.
139.event: The hero marries the five hundred Vidyadhara women, and their brothers become his attendants.

140.reading: The text introduces Ratnapura in Kalinga, its king Chandragupta, queen Chandramati and their daughter Madanamanjari.
140.nuance: Like 128 and 142, a city-and-king introduction with no verb.

141.reading: By the mantra-rite the hero reaches Madanamanjari, rides in her company and drinks deeply of her, their union like that of a nagas' pair.
141.nuance: The simile of the last line (நாகநற் புணர்ச்சிபோல்) plays on the hero's name Naga; the line 3 phrase தான்லயப் பருகினான் is read as drinking in desire.
141.event: The hero marries Madanamanjari by a mantra-rite and enjoys her.

142.reading: The text introduces Tilakapura in the land of Kangala, its king Vijayandhara and his wife Iyalvisai.
142.nuance: Another introduction in the series of city-and-king verses (128, 140, 142).

143.reading: The hero goes to Ilakkanai, their daughter, wins her at once by the rite and takes her pleasure, when ancient sages come to the grove.
143.nuance: The mantra-rite is called a matter of truth (மெய்ம்மை வேள்வி), the poem's claim that this is a true way of winning a bride.
143.event: The hero marries Ilakkanai and enjoys her; ancient sages arrive at the grove.

144.reading: The hero bows to the sage of firm austerity, hears the dharma that suits him, and asks what the high pleasure of Ilakkanai has been, which the sage will explain.
144.nuance: The sage's answer is not in this verse (the sentence ends with the promise to teach); the question is about the cause of that fortune in a former birth, as the next verses will show, but this verse says only ஏற்றமோகம் என்ன.
144.event: The hero bows to the Charana sage, hears dharma and asks about his pleasure with Ilakkanai.

links.note: The hero kills Vayuvegan to avenge a father's murder; the couplet makes not killing the whole of virtuous action.
links.teaches: A Jain-framed epic lets its hero kill a usurper without comment, so the couplet's absolute not-killing meets a case where the story itself counts killing as justice.

gains.a: the hero's killing is seen against a rule the poem's own faith holds
gains.b: the couplet is shown meeting a hard case of vengeance for murder

links.note: Vayuvegan kills a king and seizes his land; the hero kills him, as the king's weeding of the cruel in the couplet.
links.teaches: The couplet puts the punishment of the cruel in a king's hand; here a wandering prince does it, so the story shows the same duty fallen to whoever happens to be there.

gains.a: the hero's killing is read as the weeding-out of a cruel man
gains.b: the couplet's weeding is shown done by a prince with no throne

links.note: The hero takes five hundred princesses by the mantra-rite; the couplet praises the man who does not look at another's wife.
links.teaches: The couplet bars only another's wife, and the poem's heroes win unmarried women, so the epic's polygamy sits outside what the couplet forbids.

gains.a: the hero's many marriages are measured against the couplet's one fixed limit
gains.b: the couplet's limit is shown to leave room for many wives who are unmarried

links.note: The merchant could not say why five hundred women sing daily at the temple; Dharanisundari gives the cause.
links.teaches: The merchant's wonder is only a wonder until the women speak, showing the poem makes a marvel into a wrong that the hero is to put right.

links.note: Just after the hero takes his pleasure with Ilakkanai, sages arrive and he asks them about it.
links.teaches: The sage's coming in the same breath as the marriage shows the poem placing the hero's pleasures under the teaching that follows them.

source_issues: Verse 124 to 125 have corrupt lines (124 lines 1-2, 125 line 3) and the story cannot be fixed from them.
Verses 129 and 130 do not say plainly whose brother Mavyalan is, or who asks the question in 130.
Verse 128 line 3 was repaired by the build (pulli after a vowel sign removed).
